---
title: "Railroad Man (鉄道員)"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-09-09"
categories: [realization]
---

I was spending time in the city-state, located 93 miles north of the equator, helping the local team develop and strengthen its R&D operations.

Four of us from Utah would make a series of the 8,900-mile journey, staying for two to three weeks at a time.

Although the city was organized and clean, with all of the desirable items for sale, there was only so much shopping and eating one can do before the novelty wears off and the island fever sets in.

I found myself, after 3rd or 4th visit, looking for meaningful ways to pass the weekend hours.

Luckily, a Japanese Film Festival provided that relief.[^1]

[^1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Film_Festival

It was there that I saw *Poppoya* (*Railroad Man*), a 1999 Japanese drama directed by 降旗 康男 (Yasuo Furuhata).[^2], [Japanese Wiki](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%89%84%E9%81%93%E5%93%A1_(%E5%B0%8F%E8%AA%AC))

[^2]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poppoya

The film stars Ken Takakura (高倉 健) as Otomatsu Sato, a devoted railway stationmaster in the remote, snowbound town of Horomai in Hokkaido.

As he prepares to retire after decades of service, Otomatsu reflects on a life defined by unwavering duty to the railway—and the heavy personal sacrifices that came with it, including the tragic losses of his wife and young daughter.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The film was not just a weekend entertainment; it changed my outlook on life, as a young father raising a family.

Sitting in a theater thousands of miles from home, with Sister K taking care of child and handling household affairs so I can travel, the movie hit deep vulnerabilities.

It forced me to confront things I had too often sidelined: taking my wife for granted, or not spending enough time with my children—especially my daughter.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Those quiet regrets were handled in the film with a haunting tenderness.

Later in the movie, when a young woman appear to Otomatsu—who resembles what his own daughter would have looked like had she grown up—it elevated the narrative to another level entirely.

Woven into the film is the familiar America-based melody of the *Tennessee Waltz*, written by Redd Stewart and Pee Wee King and made famous by Patti Page.[^3]

[^3]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Waltz

Without reliance on words, the meaning of life was told: framed by Japanese actors in the silence of Hokkaido, raw feelings enhanced by an American song from 1950.[A YouTube Video Clip](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UN-Ax0xdK6Y)

In that theater, the demands and limits of work duty were shown, as well its effects, and what many of us take for granted was taught anew.
